items.title: Cooking with Anna Haugh: ‘A langoustine is easy to make outstanding, but a carrot takes skill’
items.summary:
The MasterChef judge on artichokes, ambition and Irish food

It’s an amazing moment when Anna Haugh lets me peel and chop a butternut squash, right there in the kitchen next to her, while she makes a beetroot pickle. The 46-year-old is a fiendish perfectionist and a fierce champion of every last ingredient. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle, named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen. It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop.

Elite cooking while talking like a Bren gun is a skill she’s honed, first in cookery demos “talking to a plastic bag and a stray dog, and you’d be lucky if someone came over to shelter from the rain”; then on Saturday Kitchen – a trial by fire: “Everything is easy after that. I could do any cookery programme now. I even tried to persuade them to do the MasterChef final live.”
items.t: Cooking with Anna Haugh: ‘A langoustine is easy to make outstanding, but a carrot takes skill’

items.title: Where does the pope do his big shop?​ And is he buying white beans this week?
items.summary:
​I set out to visit the supermarket in Vatican City and discovered who can actually shop there and what they might be cooking

A couple of years ago, it was announced that the supermarket inside Vatican City was to be taken over by the Gabrielli group and become one of their medium-sized Tigre stores “known for daily freshness and a welcoming and courteous atmosphere”. I remember reading this announcement in Roma Today and assuming the new supermarket would be like the impeccably efficient Vatican post office and open to everyone, and that one day I would share a freezer aisle with cardinals, nuns and off-duty Swiss Guards.

Fast forward two years to the Feast team’s discovery that Vatican City is one of two countries in which there are no Feast app users (the other is North Korea). “What do they eat in Vatican City?” was the next question. Bingo, I thought, knowing exactly where Vatican residents do at least some of their shopping. Here was my chance to shop and to investigate, and to see if the special offers at our local Tigre are the same as in Papa Leo XIV’s hood in Vatican City, the smallest independent state in the world.

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for bread buns with cheese and apple | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary:
Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol

In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery, there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat.

It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet.

items.summary:
Forgive the Daddy Warbucks-ness of what I’m about to say, but I think it’s important to remember that a splurge and an extravagance aren’t quite the same thing when it comes to gifts. On one end of the spectrum, there are vapid luxury items; on the other, there are the gifts whose steeper price point is tied directly to their artistry, quality, and/or durability. While the former can be fun to window-shop, our hard-earned clams are best spent on the latter. 

As a seasoned shopping writer, I ask myself two big questions when mulling over a pricey purchase: What is the story behind this item? Can I picture it in my life for years to come? 

Consider the iconic, mid-century modern Moccamaster coffee machine , which first debuted in the 1960s and has been trending on social media lately for its array of colorful, modular designs. I took the cult-fave machine for an extended test run (it’s still my daily driver), and the yellow pepper iteration made me fall in love with drip coffee all over again. The Dutch company behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year , and Chicago’s Bad Butter , a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries . Instead of storming the gates of department stores at dawn for Salad Shooters and Cabbage Patch dolls, we now sit on our own couches to peruse the deals online — and there are lots of deals . items.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail
items.summary:
Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch

What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party?
Dan, by email
We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals. The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all associate with the festive season”.

items.title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
items.summary:
Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done

Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls.

The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner.
items.t: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
